title: Composition and occasion
short: Dated 'at Stoke Aug: 1742' in Gray's Commonplace Book; published anonymously by Dodsley on 30 May 1747, Gray's first English poem in print.
body: Gray's transcript in his Commonplace Book is dated 'at Stoke, Aug: 1742' and titled 'Ode, on a distant Prospect of Windsor, & the adjacent Country'; Eton is not named. It was printed anonymously by Dodsley as a sixpenny folio on 30 May 1747, then under Gray's name in Dodsley's Collection of Poems (1748). The summer of 1742 was a dark one: Richard West, Gray's closest Eton friend, died on 1 June, and Gray was uncertain of his own future. Lonsdale notes that Eton and Windsor could actually be seen from Stoke Poges, so the 'prospect' is literal as well as a view back in time. A letter of May 1742 recalls his schoolfellows as 'dirty boys playing at cricket', and Lonsdale argues that Gray, who had avoided the rough games, could idealise a childhood he watched from a distance.

anchor: Anthrôpos, hikanê prophasis eis to dustuchein
title: the epigraph from Menander
greek: Greek ánthrōpos: hikanḕ próphasis eis tò dystycheîn
short: 'I am a man: sufficient reason for being unhappy.' A fragment of the Greek comic poet Menander, added as the motto in 1768.
body: The Greek, transliterated in the archive, reads ánthrōpos: hikanḕ próphasis eis tò dystycheîn, 'a man: a sufficient excuse for being unhappy'. It is a fragment of Menander (c. 342-290 BC), the master of Athenian New Comedy, preserved in later anthologies; editors cite it among his fragments. The motto stands in the margin beside the fifth and sixth stanzas in Gray's manuscripts, near 'Ah, tell them, they are men!' (l. 60), which it glosses, and it was first printed with the poem in 1768 (Poems by Mr. Gray). A comic poet's shrug becomes the text for an elegy on human life.

title: antique towers ... crown the watery glade
short: 'Antique' means ancient; the towers of Eton College crown the riverside meadows, in phrases gathered from Milton and Pope.
body: Bradshaw notes that 'antique' here simply means ancient, the sense it has in Milton's 'antick Pillars' (Il Penseroso 158). Lonsdale gathers the sources of the opening: Comus 934-5 ('May thy lofty head be crown'd / With many a tower'), Pope's Windsor Forest ('Windsor-Domes and pompous Turrets', and 'haunt the watry Glade'), and Dyer's Grongar Hill ('ancient towers crown his brow'). A 'glade' is an open space among trees; 'watery' because the college lies on the Thames meadows. The opening is thus a topographical poem in the tradition of Denham's Cooper's Hill and Pope's Windsor Forest, before it turns personal.

title: Science
short: Knowledge or learning in general, personified as grateful to the college's founder.
body: As in the Elegy's 'Fair Science frown'd not on his humble birth', 'Science' means knowledge or learning at large, the older sense of Latin scientia, not natural science. Tovey, Lonsdale and Reeves all gloss it so. Learning is 'grateful' because it owes its home at Eton to Henry VI, and it 'still' (always, to this day) 'adores' his memory. The personification sets the poem's method: abstractions become actors, a technique the ode will push much further in its catalogue of passions.

title: Henry's holy shade
short: Henry VI (1421-71), who founded Eton in 1440, was revered as a saintly king; 'shade' means both his ghost and the shade of the trees.
body: Gray's own note identifies Henry VI as the founder of the college. Lonsdale records that a statue of the king had been placed in School Yard shortly before Gray arrived in 1725, and that Gray elsewhere stresses his sanctity (The Bard, l. 90; Ode for Music); Shakespeare calls him 'holy Henry' in Richard III, and Pope calls him 'the Martyr-King' in Windsor Forest. Henry was murdered in the Tower in 1471 and venerated as a martyr. 'Shade' combines the classical sense of a departed spirit (Latin umbra) with the literal shade of the college groves, so the founder's ghost presides over the landscape.

title: Windsor's heights
short: Windsor Castle on its hill across the Thames from Eton, from which the eye surveys grove, lawn and meadow.
body: The 'ye' of l. 5 addresses the towers of Windsor Castle, which stand on a chalk hill above the river opposite Eton; from their 'stately brow' they survey the wide view below. Gray's first title made Windsor, not Eton, the subject ('a distant Prospect of Windsor, & the adjacent Country'). The Commonplace Book reads 'Of Grove & Lawn & Mead survey'. Lonsdale compares Pope's Summer, where Thames winds through forests and flowery meads; the triple 'whose turf, whose shade, whose flowers' imitates the panoramic sweep of a prospect poem.

title: the hoary Thames and his silver-winding way
greek: Latin tardis ingens ubi flexibus errat / Mincius
short: The river is an old man, white-haired ('hoary'), wandering in silver windings like Virgil's Mincius.
body: Rivers were traditionally imagined as aged gods (Phelps cites Pope's 'Old father Thames' and Spenser's 'full-aged' Thame), hence 'hoary'. Lonsdale points to Virgil's Mincius, which 'wanders in slow windings' (Georgics III.14-15, tardis ingens ubi flexibus errat), and notes that 'silver' is a stock epithet for the Thames in Spenser, Dryden, Pope and Thomson. The verb 'Wanders' prepares the boys who 'stray' and the 'bold adventurers' who range beyond bounds: the river's leisurely course is an image of the carefree time the poem mourns.

title: belov'd in vain
short: The fields are loved without return: they cannot restore his lost childhood, and, for many editors, they recall Richard West, newly dead.
body: Why 'in vain'? Bradshaw explains that the fields no longer give the poet the feelings he had as a 'careless' boy, and adds a reference to West's death in June 1742. Gosse, quoted by Tovey, read the phrase as Gray's half-hidden grief for his lost friend. Lonsdale links the phrase to the Sonnet on the Death of Richard West, written the same month, which ends 'And weep the more, because I weep in vain'. Readers who resist biography take the phrase more generally: the love of a place cannot bring back the time spent in it. Lonsdale also cites Gay's Rural Sports, 'Ye happy fields ... where once I us'd to rove', as a model for the apostrophe.

title: redolent of joy and youth
short: The breezes smell of, and so recall, joy and youth; Gray's note cites Dryden's 'honey redolent of spring'. Johnson thought the phrase strained.
body: 'Redolent' (Latin redolere, to give off a smell) means fragrant with, and by extension evocative of. Gray's own note cites Dryden's version of Ovid, Metamorphoses XV ('Of the Pythagorean Philosophy'), where honey is 'redolent of spring'. Johnson complained in his Life of Gray that Dryden's phrase was already at the limit of the language and that Gray pushed it further, making gales 'redolent of joy and youth'. The breezes 'seem' to soothe and to breathe 'a second spring': the momentary bliss of l. 16 is already qualified. Lonsdale compares Aaron Hill's Solitude, which welcomes a cool breeze to a mind burnt by cares.

title: Say, Father Thames
short: Gray asks the river-god who now plays on his banks, echoing Matthew Green's The Grotto; Johnson found the question 'useless and puerile'.
body: Lonsdale traces 'Father Thames' to Dryden and Pope (Windsor Forest), but thinks Gray had in mind Matthew Green's The Grotto: 'Say, father Thames, whose gentle pace / Gives leave to view what beauties grace / Your flowery banks'. Johnson objected that Father Thames 'has no better means of knowing than himself'. Tovey called the objection frivolous: the address to the river, which has seen generations of boys ('Full many a sprightly race'), is a way of setting one life against the continuity of the place. The question also distances Gray from the present boys, whom he can name only as types.

title: margent
short: 'Margent' is an old form of 'margin', the river bank; the phrase comes from Milton's Comus.
body: Tovey notes that 'margent' is the regular form for 'margin' in Shakespeare and Milton, and that Gray recalls Comus 232, 'By slow Meander's margent green'. Reeves glosses simply 'banks'. Choosing the archaic form and a Miltonic phrase is typical of Gray's diction, which, as Johnson complained, often prefers the poetic to the common word. The boys 'disporting' (amusing themselves) on the bank trace 'the paths of pleasure', a phrase Lonsdale finds in Pope's Essay on Man.

title: the boys' games
short: The boys swim, snare linnets, bowl hoops and play ball; Gray first wrote 'the Hoop's elusive Speed' and then replaced the homely word.
body: Phelps reads the stanza as a list of school sports: swimming ('cleave ... thy glassy wave'), catching or caging birds ('captive linnet'), trundling hoops ('the rolling circle'), and ball games. The Commonplace Book reads 'To chase the Hoop's elusive Speed'; Lonsdale thinks Gray changed it to avoid echoing a phrase from his own Agrippina, while Crofts suggests that 'hoop' seemed too low a word for poetry. The periphrasis is a classic instance of eighteenth-century poetic diction. Lonsdale cites Ovid, Tristia III.xii, where Roman boys play with the ball and the swift hoop, and Pope's Dunciad, 'The Senator at Cricket urge the Ball'.

title: murmuring labours
short: The studious boys mutter their lessons aloud to learn them by heart before the 'graver hours' of school.
body: Tovey explains that the boys are 'conning by heart and repeating aloud to themselves the tasks' they must say to their masters in school; Lonsdale quotes him. Their 'earnest business' is homework, and the paradox of the couplet is that they work in their free time against the hours of constraint, 'to sweeten liberty': diligence makes the coming confinement easier, or makes the present freedom sweeter. The stanza sets three types side by side: the players, the workers and the truants.

title: the bold adventurers
short: The bolder boys break bounds into 'unknown regions', looking back as they run, startled by every sound, snatching a joy that is half fear.
body: Tovey glosses: 'They go out of bounds.' Their 'little reign' is the school's permitted ground. Lonsdale finds 'unknown regions' and 'descries' in Cowley's ode To Mr Hobbes, and for the fearful runners he cites Virgil's Aeneas, escaping Troy, startled by every breeze and sound (Aeneid II.728-9), and Pope's untutored mind that 'hears him [God] in the wind'. 'They hear a voice in every wind' (Phelps: 'the pursuing master') gives the scene a comic surface and a darker undertone, since the fear of pursuit anticipates the 'ambush' of adult misfortune later in the poem.

title: a fearful joy
short: An oxymoron: pleasure mixed with fear, after Virgil's 'joy and fear' (Aeneid I.513-14).
body: Lonsdale compares Aeneid I.513-14, where Aeneas and Achates, seeing their lost comrades, are struck with joy and fear together (laetitiaque metuque), and Silius Italicus' laeto pavore, 'joyful dread'. 'Snatch' implies haste and theft: the pleasure is stolen, brief, and taken against the rules. The phrase sums up the stanza and prepares the poem's argument, that childhood joy is real but precarious and already shadowed by fear.

title: hope less pleasing when possessed
greek: Latin sed dum abest quod avemus, id exsuperare videtur / cetera
short: The boys' hope, fed by fancy, is sweeter than its fulfilment, a thought from Lucretius III, via Dryden's translation.
body: Lonsdale cites Lucretius, De rerum natura III.1082-3: while we lack what we crave, it seems better than everything else; once we have it, we crave something else. Dryden's version gives 'For still we think an absent blessing best; / Which cloys, and is no blessing when possest', which Gray echoes almost word for word. Lonsdale also traces 'The sunshine of the breast' to Pope ('Eternal sunshine of the spotless mind', Eloisa to Abelard) and Thomson. The stanza describes childhood as an Eden of light sleep and easy days, with echoes of Adam's 'Aerie light' sleep in Paradise Lost V.

title: buxom
greek: Old English bugan, to bow (būhsum, pliant)
short: Lively, vigorous, full of health. Johnson thought Gray misunderstood the word; Tovey shows the sense had long shifted from 'obedient' to 'brisk'.
body: 'Buxom' comes from Old English bugan, to bow, and first meant pliant, obedient; by Shakespeare's time it had come to mean lively and blithe (Pistol's 'buxom valour', Henry V III.vi), and later plump and comely. Johnson objected that 'buxom health' was not elegant and that Gray seemed not to understand the word; Tovey answered that the primary sense had long been lost and that the transferred sense, prompt and lively, was established. Lonsdale glosses 'lively, healthy', and compares 'rosie red', 'Loves proper hue', in Paradise Lost VIII. Milton's 'buxom, blithe and debonair' (L'Allegro 24) is probably behind Gray's choice.

title: the little victims
short: Ignorant of their fate, the children play like sacrificial animals, while the ministers of human fate wait in ambush.
body: The stanza turns the poem: 'Alas!' Lonsdale compares Dryden's Astraea Redux, 'And Heaven that seem'd regardless of our Fate', and for 'ministers of human fate' cites Ariel's 'ministers of Fate' in The Tempest III.iii, Thomson, Otway and Broome. 'Victims' keeps its Latin sense, animals destined for sacrifice (victima), which play unaware of the knife; the image recalls Pope's lamb that 'licks the hand just rais'd to shed his blood' (Essay on Man I). The 'murtherous band' in ambush was first 'griesly' in the Commonplace Book. Lonsdale cites Spenser's 'ambushment' of hatred and murder.

anchor: Ah, tell them, they are men!
title: Ah, tell them, they are men!
short: The climax of the warning: to be human is to suffer, the thought of the Menander epigraph.
body: Gray wrote the Menander motto in the margin beside the stanzas around this line, and the two say the same thing: to be a man is reason enough for misery. The line is an imperative to an unnamed listener (Father Thames, or the reader) and it is both pitying and grim. The final stanza returns to the phrase, 'all are men, / Condemn'd alike to groan', and then retracts the wish to tell them. Readers have long noticed the tension between the urge to warn and the conclusion that warning is useless.

title: the fury Passions and the vultures of the mind
greek: Latin vestibulum ante ipsum primisque in faucibus Orci
short: The passions are Furies and vultures tearing the mind, as the vultures tear Tityos in the underworld; the catalogue descends from Virgil's figures at the gate of Hades.
body: 'The Fury-passions' is Pope's phrase (Essay on Man III), used after a description of man's lost innocence. The 'vultures of the mind' recall the vultures that feed on Tityos (or the eagle of Prometheus); Lucretius had already read the myth as an allegory of love and anxiety gnawing the living (De rerum natura III.992-4). Lonsdale notes that most English catalogues of this kind descend from Aeneid VI.273-81, where Grief, Cares, Diseases, Old Age, Fear, Hunger and Want lodge at the entrance to the underworld. Gray's procession, Anger, Fear, Shame, Love, Jealousy, Envy, Care, Despair, Sorrow, Ambition, follows that model.

title: Grim-visaged comfortless Despair
short: Gray probably fuses two Shakespeare phrases: 'Grim-visag'd war' (Richard III) and 'grim and comfortless despair' (The Comedy of Errors).
body: Tovey and Lonsdale agree that Gray combines the opening of Richard III ('Grim-visag'd war hath smooth'd his wrinkled front', I.i.9) with The Comedy of Errors V.i.80, 'grim and comfortless despair'. Lonsdale adds that Mitford found 'grim visadged dispaire' in Robert Yarington's Two Lamentable Tragedies (1601). Nearby, 'Envy wan' and 'faded Care' come from Milton (Sonnet to Henry Lawes; Paradise Lost I.601-2). The stanza shows Gray's mosaic method: almost every personification is made from remembered phrases, which gives the list the weight of tradition.

title: the painful family of Death
short: Diseases are Death's household, after Dryden's 'numerous Family of Death'; in the 'vale of years' (Othello) they await the old.
body: Lonsdale and Tovey cite Dryden's State of Innocence, where sickness, care and age, brought by Adam's crime, come 'With all the numerous Family of Death'. Tovey notes that 'family' means attendants, the household (Latin familia), not offspring. The 'vale of years' is Othello's phrase (III.iii), and the 'grisly troop' recalls Comus. The diseases are 'More hideous than their queen', since Death herself (Milton's 'queen of tombs', Lonsdale notes) ends pain while they inflict it. The stanza moves from mental to bodily suffering, ending with Poverty and 'slow-consuming Age'.

title: where ignorance is bliss, 'tis folly to be wise
short: The famous close: since knowledge of their fate cannot help them, it would be foolish to destroy the children's happiness. Editors list many parallels, none certainly Gray's source.
body: Lonsdale lists parallels without claiming that Gray used any one: Sophocles' Ajax, telling his son that knowing nothing is the sweetest life; Terence's Hecyra, that the time before we learn of trouble is pure gain; Sir William Davenant's song in The Just Italian, 'Since Knowledge is but sorrow's Spy, / It is not safe to know'; and Prior's 'The only wretched are the Wise'. The lines are often quoted as if they praised ignorance in general. In context the claim is narrow and conditional ('where'): knowledge of future suffering would only bring sorrow early. Some readers find the ending consoling; others think it undercuts the long warning before it, or reflects Gray's own melancholy rather than an argument.

title: stanza and form
short: Ten ten-line stanzas rhymed ababccdeed, mixing iambic tetrameter with trimeter; a regular Horatian ode rather than a Pindaric.
body: Each stanza has ten lines rhymed ababccdeed; lines 2, 4 and 10 are trimeters and the rest tetrameters, so each stanza opens with a lyric quatrain and closes with a shorter cadence. The structure is regular and Horatian, unlike the irregular Pindarics of the period. The movement is dramatic: two stanzas of landscape and memory; three of the boys at play; a turn at 'Alas!' (stanza 6); three stanzas of personified evils; and a closing reflection. Exclamation ('Ah, happy hills! ah, pleasing shade!') and apostrophe mark the ode's emotional register. Lonsdale emphasises the fusion of topographical poem and subjective ode.
